title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
聖其揆一也豈欺我哉請因明問而條陳之
天生斯民不能自治必作之君師使之治而
教之以復其性焉稽之於古若堯使舜為司
徒而慎徽五典舜命契為司徒而敬敷五教
以至禹之文命敷於四海湯之肇脩人紀武
王之重民五教是皆本乎躬行心得之餘而
不出於民生日用彛倫之外者也是以成雍
熈泰和之治而非後世之所能及焉自是而
後若漢之明帝唐之太宗皆願治之君也一
===
===
則尊師重傅臨雍拜老一則大召名儒增廣
生員名非不美也然教焉而不知所以教徒
有儀文之具而無躬行之實此其所以漢止
於漢唐止於唐雜覇雜夷而終不古若也洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝創業垂統脩成大誥三編所以勸善
懲惡也如君臣同遊諸官生身之恩非一條
而專指一倫者乎民不知報婚姻之條非一
條而兼舉五倫者乎
punctuated: 聖，其揆一也」，豈欺我哉？請因明問而條陳之。天生斯民，不能自治，必作之君師，使之治而教之，以復其性焉。稽之於古，若堯使舜為司徒而慎徽五典，舜命契為司徒而敬敷五教，以至禹之文命敷於四海，湯之肇脩人紀，武王之重民五教，是皆本乎躬行心得之餘，而不出於民生日用彛倫之外者也。是以成雍熈泰和之治，而非後世之所能及焉。自是而後，若漢之明帝、唐之太宗，皆願治之君也。一則尊師重傅，臨雍拜老；一則大召名儒，增廣生員。名非不美也，然教焉而不知所以教，徒有儀文之具，而無躬行之實。此其所以漢止於漢，唐止於唐，雜覇雜夷，而終不古若也。洪惟我太祖高皇帝創業垂統，脩成《大誥》三編，所以勸善懲惡也。如「君臣同遊」、「諸官生身之恩」，非一條而專指一倫者乎？「民不知報」、「婚姻」之條，非一條而兼舉五倫者乎？
translation_en:
… sages, their principles are one"—how could that deceive us? Allow me to set forth my answer item by item in response to the explicit question.

When Heaven gave birth to the people, they could not govern themselves; thus Heaven necessarily raised up for them rulers and teachers, causing them to govern and instruct the people so as to restore their innate nature. Examining antiquity, we see how Yao employed Shun as Minister of Education (situ) to carefully exemplify the five cardinal duties; how Shun commanded Xie to serve as Minister of Education to reverently spread the five teachings; and further, how Yu spread his civilizing mandate throughout the Four Seas, how Tang initiated the cultivation of human relationships, and how King Wu attached great importance to the five teachings for the people. All of these were rooted in the overflow of their personal practice and inner realization, and did not depart from the invariable human relations of the people's daily lives. Therefore, they achieved governance of harmonious prosperity and supreme peace, which later ages could never match.

From that time onward, rulers such as Emperor Ming of the Han and Taizong of the Tang were both monarchs who desired good governance. The one honored teachers and respected tutors, personally visiting the Imperial Hall of Learning (Biyong) to pay homage to the aged; the other summoned renowned Confucian scholars on a grand scale and expanded the quota of government students. Their reputations were by no means inglorious; yet while they instructed, they did not understand the true basis of instruction, possessing merely the trappings of ritual and form without the reality of personal practice. This is why the Han remained merely the Han and the Tang remained merely the Tang—adulterated by the ways of hegemons and barbarians, and ultimately failing to equal antiquity.

Looking with awe upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), he founded the dynastic enterprise and handed down its legitimate succession, compiling the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) as the means to encourage goodness and punish evil. For instance, are not entries such as "Ruler and Ministers Sharing Fellowship" and "The Grace of Parents Who Gave Birth to Officials" single articles that specifically point to a single human relationship? And are not the articles on "The People Not Knowing How to Repay Kindness" and "Marriage" single articles that simultaneously encompass all five human relationships? …

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
太宗□□繼體守成製孝順事實爲善陰隲二
書所以敦本務德也事實所載固多專言孝
者若考叔遺羹蕭固孝謹姜詩出鯉閔損單
衣與夫順之悲戀之類非兼盡他倫者乎陰
隲所載固多泛言善者若蔣王靈應魏顆從
治叔通娶啞三郎行義與夫道宗葬友之類
非切於五倫者乎
宣宗章皇帝纂集五倫一書所以申明五常也自
其善行首稱而言君則黃帝臣則伯禹父子
===
則周公旦尹伯奇也夫則冀缺妻則共姜兄
弟朋友則虞舜管鮑也夫四書之製切於斯
民之彝倫本乎
三聖之躬行與二帝三王之敎實同條而共貫也
夫何間然之有雖然二帝三王先孔子而聖
者也非孔子之刪述六經則帝王之道無所
徴矣然則先聖之道不明於孔子而誰明我
朝
三聖後孔子而聖者也非孔子之刪述六經則四
punctuated: 太宗□□繼體守成，製《孝順事實》、《爲善陰隲》二書，所以敦本務德也。《事實》所載，固多專言孝者，若考叔遺羹、蕭固孝謹、姜詩出鯉、閔損單衣，與夫順之悲戀之類，非兼盡他倫者乎？《陰隲》所載，固多泛言善者，若蔣王靈應、魏顆從治、叔通娶啞、三郎行義，與夫道宗葬友之類，非切於五倫者乎？宣宗章皇帝纂集《五倫》一書，所以申明五常也。自其善行首稱而言：君則黃帝，臣則伯禹，父子則周公旦、尹伯奇也；夫則冀缺，妻則共姜，兄弟、朋友則虞舜、管鮑也。夫四書之製，切於斯民之彝倫，本乎三聖之躬行，與二帝、三王之敎實同條而共貫也，夫何間然之有！雖然，二帝、三王，先孔子而聖者也；非孔子之刪述《六經》，則帝王之道無所徴矣。然則先聖之道，不明於孔子而誰明？我朝三聖，後孔子而聖者也；非孔子之刪述《六經》，則四
translation_en: Emperor Taizong [Yongle, r. 1402–1424] [two illegible characters, likely 文皇帝, Emperor Wen] succeeded to the sovereign body and preserved the dynastic achievement, composing the two books Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) and Secret Rewards of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi), whereby he cultivated the root and devoted himself to virtue. What is recorded in the Accounts indeed mostly speaks specifically of filial piety; yet cases such as Ying Kaoshu setting aside the soup, Xiao Gu’s filial caution, Jiang Shi and the springing carps, Min Sun’s unlined garment, and Pei Shunzhi’s grieving attachment—do they not also fulfill the other human relationships? What is recorded in the Secret Rewards indeed mostly speaks broadly of goodness; yet cases such as Prince Jiang’s numinous response, Wei Ke following his father's lucid command, He Shutong marrying a mute woman, Third Brother practicing righteousness, and Fan Daozong burying his friend—are they not pertinent to the Five Human Relationships? Emperor Xuanzong Zhang [Xuande, r. 1425–1435] compiled the single work Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu), whereby he expounded the Five Constant Virtues. Speaking from the foremost examples cited under its "Good Deeds" sections: for the ruler it is the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), for the minister it is Yu the Great (Boyu), and for father and son they are the Duke of Zhou (Dan) and Yin Boqi; for the husband it is Ji Que, for the wife it is Gong Jiang, and for brothers and friends they are Yu Shun and Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya. Now, the production of these four books is closely pertinent to the constant moral relationships of our people and rooted in the personal practice of our Three Sage Emperors; with the teachings of the Two Emperors and Three Kings they truly share the same branches and are threaded upon a single cord—what flaw could possibly be found in them! Even so, the Two Emperors and Three Kings were sages prior to Confucius; had Confucius not edited and transmitted the Six Classics, there would be nothing by which to attest the Way of those emperors and kings. Thus, if the Way of the former sages was not made luminous by Confucius, by whom could it have been made luminous? The Three Sages of our dynasty are sages subsequent to Confucius; had Confucius not edited and transmitted the Six Classics, then the four …

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
書之作無所宗矣然則後聖之書不法孔子
而誰法愚也服膺
聖訓于兹有年敢以是為復惟執事幸進而教之
第二問
吕獻
同考試官學正方批
塲中答者不過敷演問目
而已此策詳答無遺足
見學識
考試官教諭趙批考索精詳無負明經之名
===
考試官教授戴批考據詳悉蓋熟於經學者也
六經作而聖人之道有所寓諸儒出而聖人
之經有所傳蓋不有聖人之作經固無以明
斯道之所在不有諸儒之繼出又何以使聖
經傳之而不泯哉明問有及於此敢不悉心
以對昔吾夫子生當周末有德無位歷聘列
國而知道終不行故自衛反魯刪詩書定禮
樂賛周易脩春秋使六經之道昭如日星奈
何一燼於秦火而六經幾滅再鑿於漢儒而
punctuated:
書之作無所宗矣。然則後聖之書，不法孔子而誰法？愚也服膺聖訓于兹有年，敢以是為復，惟執事幸進而教之。
第二問
吕獻
同考試官學正方批：塲中答者不過敷演問目而已，此策詳答無遺，足見學識。
考試官教諭趙批：考索精詳，無負明經之名。
考試官教授戴批：考據詳悉，蓋熟於經學者也。
六經作而聖人之道有所寓，諸儒出而聖人之經有所傳。蓋不有聖人之作經，固無以明斯道之所在；不有諸儒之繼出，又何以使聖經傳之而不泯哉？明問有及於此，敢不悉心以對？昔吾夫子生當周末，有德無位，歷聘列國而知道終不行，故自衛反魯，刪《詩》、《書》，定《禮》、《樂》，賛《周易》，脩《春秋》，使六經之道昭如日星。奈何一燼於秦火，而六經幾滅；再鑿於漢儒，而
translation_en:
… Books would have had nothing to take as their ancestral model. That being so, if the books of the later sages did not take Confucius as their model, whom would they follow? In my simplicity, I have cherished the Sacred Instructions in my heart for years now, and I venture to offer this as my reply, hoping only that Your Excellency will graciously admit me and instruct me.

Second Question
Lü Xian 呂獻
Comment by Associate Examiner Subprefectural Xuezbeng (Director of Studies) Fang: Those answering in the examination hall mostly did no more than elaborate upon the wording of the question; this policy essay answers in full detail without omission, which is sufficient to show the candidate's learning and insight.
Comment by Examiner District Director of Studies (Jiaoyu) Zhao: His investigation and research are precise and detailed, truly living up to the title of a master of the Classics (mingjing).
Comment by Examiner Prefectural Director of Studies (Jiaoshou) Dai: His textual research and evidence are thorough and comprehensive; he is surely one well-versed in classical learning.

When the Six Classics were created, the Way of the sages had something in which to lodge; when the various Confucian scholars emerged, the Classics of the sages had a means by which to be transmitted. Indeed, had the sages not created the Classics, there would certainly have been no way to make clear where this Way resides; and had the various scholars not successively emerged, how could the sacred Classics have been transmitted without perishing? Since your perceptive question touches upon this, how could I dare not devote my whole heart to replying? In antiquity, our Master was born at the end of the Zhou dynasty. Possessing virtue but lacking high position, he traveled from state to state and realized that the Way could ultimately not be put into practice. Therefore, upon returning from Wei to Lu, he pared down the Odes (Shi) and the Documents (Shu), fixed the Rites (Li) and Music (Yue), wrote commentaries on the Changes of Zhou (Zhouyi), and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), causing the Way of the Six Classics to shine as brightly as the sun and stars. Yet how regrettable that they were first reduced to ashes in the fires of Qin, so that the Six Classics were nearly extinguished, and were then subjected to forced interpretations by the Confucian scholars of the Han, so that…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
源流異别故以易而言之自商瞿學於孔子
五傳而至田何田何之後有施讐孟喜梁丘
賀之徒並立博士又有京房費氏所宗之學
至於後漢陳元鄭康成皆傳費氏易費氏興
而諸家息故王弼得於費氏而高談理致焉
若謂其得孔子授商瞿之旨則吾不知也以
書而言之自伏生作尚書四十一傳以授同
郡張生張生授歐陽生再傳而有夏侯勝建
之徒及遭永嘉之亂而是書並亡惟孔安國
===
以壁中之書考論文義定其可知故後世獨
宗之焉至若言詩者則有齊魯韓毛之四家
也魯詩始於申培而盛於韋賢齊詩始於轅
固而盛於匡衡韓詩起於韓嬰而盛於王吉
毛詩起於毛萇而傳於徐敖然毛詩雖最後
出而未顯而鄭康成馬融之徒皆發明之故
毛詩盛行而三家寖微矣但為小序牽制多
失本旨豈能有得孔子授子夏之旨歟傳春
秋者則有左氏公羊穀梁鄒氏郼氏之五家
punctuated: 源流異别。故以《易》而言之：自商瞿學於孔子，五傳而至田何；田何之後，有施讐、孟喜、梁丘賀之徒，並立博士；又有京房、費氏所宗之學。至於後漢，陳元、鄭康成皆傳費氏《易》，費氏興而諸家息，故王弼得於費氏而高談理致焉。若謂其得孔子授商瞿之旨，則吾不知也。以《書》而言之：自伏生作《尚書》四十一傳，以授同郡張生，張生授歐陽生，再傳而有夏侯勝、建之徒，及遭永嘉之亂，而是書並亡；惟孔安國以壁中之書考論文義，定其可知，故後世獨宗之焉。至若言《詩》者，則有齊、魯、韓、毛之四家也。魯《詩》始於申培而盛於韋賢，齊《詩》始於轅固而盛於匡衡，韓《詩》起於韓嬰而盛於王吉，毛《詩》起於毛萇而傳於徐敖。然毛《詩》雖最後出而未顯，而鄭康成、馬融之徒皆發明之，故毛《詩》盛行而三家寖微矣。但為《小序》牽制，多失本旨，豈能有得孔子授子夏之旨歟？傳《春秋》者，則有左氏、公羊、穀梁、鄒氏、郼氏之五家
translation_en:
…their origins and currents diverged and became distinct. Thus, to speak of the Book of Changes (Yi): from Shang Qu, who studied under Confucius, it was transmitted through five generations to Tian He. After Tian He, there were followers such as Shi Chou, Meng Xi, and Liangqiu He, whose traditions were all established under Erudites (boshi); there were also the schools revered by Jing Fang and Master Fei [Fei Zhi]. By the Later Han, Chen Yuan and Zheng Kangcheng [Zheng Xuan] both transmitted Master Fei's Changes; as Master Fei's school flourished, the other schools died out, and thus Wang Bi drew upon Master Fei to engage in lofty discourses on principle and meaning. As for whether this captured the purport that Confucius imparted to Shang Qu, that I do not know.

To speak of the Book of Documents (Shu): from Master Fu [Fu Sheng], who composed the forty-one traditions [chapters of the Great Commentary] on the Venerated Documents (Shangshu) and imparted them to Master Zhang of the same commandery, Master Zhang imparted them to Master Ouyang, and after two more transmissions there were followers such as Xiahou Sheng and [Xiahou] Jian. When the upheaval of the Yongjia era (307–313) befell, these texts all perished; only Kong Anguo used the texts from inside the wall to examine and discuss the textual meanings, establishing what could be understood, and therefore later generations exclusively revered his version.

As for those who expounded the Book of Odes (Shi), there were the four schools of Qi, Lu, Han, and Mao. The Lu Odes began with Shen Pei and flourished under Wei Xian; the Qi Odes began with Yuan Gu and flourished under Kuang Heng; the Han Odes arose with Han Ying and flourished under Wang Ji; the Mao Odes arose with Mao Chang and were transmitted to Xu Ao. Yet although the Mao Odes appeared last and was not yet prominent, scholars such as Zheng Kangcheng and Ma Rong all elucidated it, so that the Mao Odes prevailed widely while the other three schools gradually declined. However, constrained by the Lesser Prefaces (Xiaoxu), they often lost the original meaning—how could they have attained the purport that Confucius imparted to Zixia?

As for those who transmitted the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), there were the five schools of Zuo, Gongyang, Guliang, Master Zou, and Master Jia [written 郼]…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
也鄒氏無師郟氏無書故其傳泯焉惟三家
迭為盛衰祖公羊者則有胡毋生董仲舒公
孫弘祖穀梁者則有申公瑕丘江公皆傳之
於先其後傳之者少故先盛而後衰左氏自
張蒼賈誼數家之傳至劉歆始著故始微而
終盛其後杜預之集解則左氏之學也何休
之註則公羊之學也范甯之集解則又得於
穀梁之學焉以言乎禮其經有二曰周禮者
周公制太平之迹也曰禮記者孔子弟子共
===
撰所聞以為記也周禮由漢武帝購求遺典
而得於河間獻王所獻以入於祕府至劉歆
校書首先好之奏立學官當時惟鄭興能明
其義及鄭重為周官傳鄭玄為周官註故其
學遂行焉禮記本於高堂生受儀禮於蕭奮
傳之孟卿孟卿傳之后蒼后蒼傳之戴德戴
勝二戴因習儀禮而錄之於是鄭玄之徒為
之註孔穎達之輩為之疏至宋王安石始以
設科取士故其學遂盛行焉至於樂經始廢
punctuated: 也。鄒氏無師，郟氏無書，故其傳泯焉；惟三家迭為盛衰。祖《公羊》者，則有胡毋生、董仲舒、公孫弘；祖《穀梁》者，則有申公、瑕丘江公。皆傳之於先，其後傳之者少，故先盛而後衰。《左氏》自張蒼、賈誼數家之傳，至劉歆始著，故始微而終盛。其後杜預之《集解》，則《左氏》之學也；何休之《註》，則《公羊》之學也；范甯之《集解》，則又得於《穀梁》之學焉。以言乎《禮》，其經有二：曰《周禮》者，周公制太平之迹也；曰《禮記》者，孔子弟子共撰所聞以為記也。《周禮》由漢武帝購求遺典，而得於河間獻王所獻，以入於祕府。至劉歆校書，首先好之，奏立學官，當時惟鄭興能明其義。及鄭重為《周官傳》，鄭玄為《周官註》，故其學遂行焉。《禮記》本於高堂生，受《儀禮》於蕭奮，傳之孟卿，孟卿傳之后蒼，后蒼傳之戴德、戴勝，二戴因習《儀禮》而錄之。於是鄭玄之徒為之註，孔穎達之輩為之疏。至宋王安石始以設科取士，故其學遂盛行焉。至於《樂經》，始廢
translation_en:
… [five schools]. The Zou (鄒氏) school had no masters and the Jia (郟氏) school had no written texts, so their transmissions died out; only the other three schools rose and fell by turns. Those who followed the Gongyang Commentary (Gongyang 公羊) included Master Humu (Humu Sheng 胡毋生), Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒, and Gongsun Hong 公孫弘; those who followed the Guliang Commentary (Guliang 穀梁) included Master Shen (Shen Gong 申公) and Master Jiang of Xiaqiu (Xiaqiu Jiang Gong 瑕丘江公). Both were transmitted early on, but later had few who passed them down, and thus they flourished at first and declined afterward. The Zuo Commentary (Zuoshi 左氏), transmitted through several masters such as Zhang Cang 張蒼 and Jia Yi 賈誼, first became prominent only with Liu Xin 劉歆, and thus was obscure at the start and flourished in the end. Later, the Collected Explanations (Jijie 集解) of Du Yu 杜預 represented the scholarship of the Zuo Commentary; the Commentary (Zhu 註) of He Xiu 何休 represented the scholarship of the Gongyang Commentary; and the Collected Explanations (Jijie 集解) of Fan Ning 范甯 in turn derived from the scholarship of the Guliang Commentary.

As for the Rites (Li 禮), there are two classics: the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli 周禮), which is the trace of the Duke of Zhou's (Zhou Gong 周公) institution of Great Peace; and the Record of Rites (Liji 禮記), which the disciples of Confucius jointly compiled as a record of what they had heard. The Rites of Zhou was obtained when Emperor Wu of Han (Han Wudi 漢武帝) sought out surviving classics and received it as a presentation from King Xian of Hejian (Hejian Xian Wang 河間獻王), whereupon it entered the Imperial Library (Mifu 祕府). When Liu Xin collated the books, he was the first to favor it and memorialized to establish Erudites (Xueguan 學官) for it; at the time, only Zheng Xing 鄭興 was able to elucidate its meaning. When Zheng Zhong 鄭重 [i.e., 鄭眾] wrote the Commentary on the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan zhuan 周官傳) and Zheng Xuan 鄭玄 wrote the Commentary on the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan zhu 周官註), its scholarship subsequently circulated. The Record of Rites originated with Master Gaotang (Gaotang Sheng 高堂生); after Xiao Fen 蕭奮 received [or transmitted] the Etiquette and Rites (Yili 儀禮) [?], it was passed to Meng Qing 孟卿, Meng Qing passed it to Hou Cang 后蒼, and Hou Cang passed it to Dai De 戴德 and Dai Sheng 戴勝 [i.e., 戴聖]. Through practicing the Etiquette and Rites, the two Dais recorded it. Thereupon Zheng Xuan and his followers wrote commentaries (zhu 註) on it, and Kong Yingda 孔穎達 and his peers wrote subcommentaries (shu 疏) for it. By the Song dynasty, Wang Anshi 王安石 first used it to establish an examination category for selecting scholars, and so its scholarship flourished widely. As for the Classic of Music (Yuejing 樂經), it first fell into disuse…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
於周末孔子盖嘗是正再壊於秦火後世遂
失其傳說者謂禮記中之樂記即古樂經恐
此特樂經中之一篇耳所謂存十一於千百
者豈全書也耶若宋蔡西山之律呂新書亦
可以補樂經之殘缺焉愚生才疎學淺而欲
備論諸經之傳授興廢亦已難矣姑述其槩
如此未知是否
第三問
李寅
===
同考試官教諭侯批條答詳明作手也
考試官教諭趙批此答謂弭灾之道在於盡人
事以勝天時脩德以召和氣有識之士也
考試官教授戴批敷陳通暢不為問目所窘
對有氣化之適然有人事之當然夫氣化之
適然者不可必人事之當然者所可為也此
水之為患固有關於氣化而亦不可不責之
人事也歟請因明問所及而條陳之粤若陶
唐之時水猶未得所歸是以洪水横流氾濫
punctuated:
於周末，孔子盖嘗是正，再壊於秦火，後世遂失其傳。說者謂《禮記》中之《樂記》即古《樂經》，恐此特《樂經》中之一篇耳，所謂存十一於千百者，豈全書也耶？若宋蔡西山之《律呂新書》，亦可以補《樂經》之殘缺焉。愚生才疎學淺，而欲備論諸經之傳授興廢，亦已難矣！姑述其槩如此，未知是否？

第三問
李寅
同考試官教諭侯批：條答詳明，作手也。
考試官教諭趙批：此答謂弭灾之道，在於盡人事以勝天時，脩德以召和氣，有識之士也。
考試官教授戴批：敷陳通暢，不為問目所窘。

對：有氣化之適然，有人事之當然。夫氣化之適然者不可必，人事之當然者所可為也。此水之為患，固有關於氣化，而亦不可不責之人事也歟！請因明問所及而條陳之。粤若陶唐之時，水猶未得所歸，是以洪水横流，氾濫
translation_en:
…at the end of the Zhou dynasty; although Confucius had once rectified it, it was destroyed again in the fires of Qin, and later generations consequently lost its transmission. Commentators say that the Record of Music (Yueji 樂記) in the Record of Rites (Liji 禮記) is the ancient Classic of Music (Yuejing 樂經); I fear this is merely a single chapter from the Classic of Music—what is called preserving one or two out of hundreds or thousands—so how could it be the complete book? As for the New Book of Pitch-Pipes (Lülü xinshu 律呂新書) by Cai Xishan 蔡西山 [Cai Yuanding 蔡元定] of the Song, it too can supplement the fragmentary omissions of the Classic of Music. I, an ignorant student, am sparse in talent and shallow in learning, and to wish to discuss thoroughly the transmission, rise, and decline of all the Classics is indeed difficult! For now I have stated their general outline like this, not knowing whether it is correct or not.

Third Question
Li Yin 李寅
Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Hou 侯 comments: Itemized responses are detailed and clear; the work of a skilled hand.
Examiner, Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: This response states that the way to avert disaster lies in exhausting human effort to overcome the seasons of Heaven, and cultivating virtue to summon harmonious ether; he is a scholar of insight.
Examiner, Instructor (jiaoshou) Dai 戴 comments: The exposition is fluent and unimpeded, not constrained by the sub-topics of the question.

Response: There is the fortuitousness of the transformations of ether (qihua 氣化), and there is what ought to be done in human affairs. Now, what is fortuitous in the transformations of ether cannot be counted upon with certainty, whereas what ought to be done in human affairs is something that can be accomplished. Thus the disasters caused by floods surely have to do with the transformations of ether, yet can we fail to hold human affairs responsible for them as well? Allow me to set this forth item by item following what the brilliant question has touched upon. Looking back to the time of Taotang 陶唐 [Emperor Yao 堯], the waters had not yet found their proper course; therefore the floodwaters flowed unchecked, inundating…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
於天下堯猶憂焉使禹治之順其自然之性
盡其疏鑿之功然後人得平土而居焉當是
時也欽若昊天敬授人時孰謂參賛之道有
未至哉世厎雍熙民無菜色又孰謂洚洞之
水能為害哉若我兩浙乃江南大藩地瀕海
隅歲月推遷堰堤頹圮豈能無穿齧之虞曩
歲江濤汹湧海水泛濫瀕海居民一激而廬
舍已去再至而禾稼蕩然雖其氣化之適然
抑亦人事之未預也藩臬重臣以為民患引
===
咎自歸同心協力堤之衝突者輸公家之帑
以備治之民之飢饉者發倉廩之粟以賑恤
之由是困者漸舒患者漸息事聞
當宁以斯民為念惻然于懷特命近臣以宣德意
恩至渥也雖然事不可以不預安不可以忘危
伊欲永無衝激之患可不堅捍築之功乎奈
何群議紛然各持已見司民牧者則曰勞民
傷財在於得已獨不曰因民之所利而利之
乎談世故者則曰時數使然人力難勝獨不
punctuated: 於天下。堯猶憂焉，使禹治之，順其自然之性，盡其疏鑿之功，然後人得平土而居焉。當是時也，欽若昊天，敬授人時，孰謂參賛之道有未至哉？世厎雍熙，民無菜色，又孰謂洚洞之水能為害哉？若我兩浙，乃江南大藩，地瀕海隅，歲月推遷，堰堤頹圮，豈能無穿齧之虞？曩歲江濤汹湧，海水泛濫，瀕海居民，一激而廬舍已去，再至而禾稼蕩然。雖其氣化之適然，抑亦人事之未預也。藩臬重臣以為民患，引咎自歸，同心協力。堤之衝突者，輸公家之帑以備治之；民之飢饉者，發倉廩之粟以賑恤之。由是困者漸舒，患者漸息。事聞，當宁以斯民為念，惻然于懷，特命近臣以宣德意，恩至渥也。雖然，事不可以不預，安不可以忘危。伊欲永無衝激之患，可不堅捍築之功乎？奈何群議紛然，各持已見。司民牧者則曰：「勞民傷財，在於得已。」獨不曰因民之所利而利之乎？談世故者則曰：「時數使然，人力難勝。」獨不
translation_en:
…across all under Heaven. Yao was worried about this and ordered Yu to control them. Yu followed their natural tendencies and exhausted his efforts in dredging and channeling, after which the people obtained level land on which to dwell. At that time, there was reverent accordance with August Heaven and respectful bestowal of the seasons upon the people—who could say that the way of assisting in the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth had not reached its utmost? The world attained harmonious prosperity, and the people had no famished complexions—who, again, could say that the vast and boundless waters were able to cause harm?

As for our region of Liangzhe, it is a great province south of the Yangtze, its land bordering a corner of the sea. As the months and years pass by, the weirs and dikes collapse into ruin; how could there be no danger of breaching and erosion? In a recent year, the river waves surged violently and the sea waters overflowed. For the residents along the coast, with the first surge their houses were swept away, and when the waters came a second time their standing grain was completely wiped out. Although this was a chance occurrence of cosmic transformations, was it not also because human preparations had not been made in advance? The senior provincial administrative and judicial officials regarded the people's suffering as their own, took the blame upon themselves, and worked together with one heart and united strength. Where dikes were breached by the rushing waters, they contributed funds from the public treasury to repair and put them in order; where the people suffered from famine, they opened the granaries and distributed grain to relieve and succor them. Because of this, those in distress were gradually eased, and the calamity gradually subsided. When the matter was reported to the throne, the reigning Sovereign, keeping these people in mind and feeling deep compassion in His heart, specially commissioned a close minister to proclaim His benevolent intentions—a grace most generous indeed!

Even so, affairs cannot be left unprepared for in advance, and in times of peace one cannot forget danger. If we wish to be forever free from the calamity of surging and battering waters, how can we not strengthen the work of building protective sea walls? Why is it, then, that the discussions of the multitude are so confused and divided, with each person clinging to his own view? Those in charge of governing the people say, "To toil the people and waste wealth is something that should be refrained from when possible." Yet do they alone not recall the saying, "Benefit the people on the basis of what is beneficial to them"? Meanwhile, those who talk of worldly affairs say, "It is brought about by the fate of the times; human strength can hardly overcome it." Yet do they alone not…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
能以理輔智預為障塞乎嗚呼作舍道傍三
年不成謂其言之者衆也使或潮勢復來則
前之議者特揖遜救焚徐行拯溺者也夫何
補哉必也不入無稽之言務在息民之患相
其地勢之宜循其已然之跡宜脩築者則爰
加脩築宜更張者則設法更張可費而費何
嫌於議論之不一可勞而勞何避夫怨謗之
有歸而又精選廉幹有司以董其事為監司
者時從而督察之責以程限期於必成將見
===
紓今日之急成無窮之利也若求其本則又
在於感召天地之和而不假脩治之力焉洪
惟我
皇上嗣大歷服敬天勤民慮脩德行仁有未至則
脩省以祈天慮用刑行罰有未當則命官以
審録其於欽承天道之意靡所不至然而休
徵雖迭應而灾沴亦間有者吾知天心仁愛
之意殆欲其心始是終是而純亦不已焉則
四靈畢至重譯來王而海晏波澄矣尚何灾
punctuated:
能以理輔智，預為障塞乎？嗚呼！「作舍道傍，三年不成」，謂其言之者衆也。使或潮勢復來，則前之議者，特揖遜救焚、徐行拯溺者也，夫何補哉！必也不入無稽之言，務在息民之患，相其地勢之宜，循其已然之跡，宜脩築者則爰加脩築，宜更張者則設法更張。可費而費，何嫌於議論之不一？可勞而勞，何避夫怨謗之有歸？而又精選廉幹有司以董其事，為監司者時從而督察之，責以程限，期於必成，將見紓今日之急，成無窮之利也。

若求其本，則又在於感召天地之和，而不假脩治之力焉。洪惟我皇上嗣大歷服，敬天勤民，慮脩德行仁有未至，則脩省以祈天；慮用刑行罰有未當，則命官以審録。其於欽承天道之意，靡所不至。然而休徵雖迭應，而灾沴亦間有者，吾知天心仁愛之意，殆欲其心始是終是，而純亦不已焉。則四靈畢至，重譯來王，而海晏波澄矣，尚何灾
translation_en:
… they not supplement wisdom with principle and build dikes and barriers in advance? Alas! "Building a house by the roadside, it is not finished in three years"—this refers to there being too many people offering opinions. Suppose the force of the tide should come again; then those who previously argued will have been merely bowing politely in deference while trying to put out a fire, or strolling leisurely to rescue the drowning. What help would that be! What is necessary is to pay no heed to unfounded talk and focus on ending the calamities of the people: survey the suitability of the terrain and follow the traces of what has already been done; where repairing and building are appropriate, proceed to repair and build; where thoroughgoing reform is appropriate, devise methods to carry out reform. Where expenditure is warranted, spend—why be deterred by disunity in discussions? Where labor is warranted, employ labor—why shrink from becoming the target of resentment and slander? Moreover, carefully select incorrupt and capable local officials to direct the work, while the surveillance officials inspect and supervise them from time to time, holding them to deadlines and insisting on sure completion. Then we shall see the urgency of the present day relieved and boundless benefit achieved.

If we seek the fundamental root of the matter, however, it lies in evoking and summoning the harmony of Heaven and Earth, without relying on the effort of repair and construction. Humbly reflecting on how Our Emperor succeeded to the great hereditary rule, he reveres Heaven and is diligent toward the people. Concerned lest the cultivation of virtue and practice of benevolence be incomplete, he engages in self-cultivation and introspection to pray to Heaven; concerned lest the application of punishments and penalties be improper, he commissions officials to review the prisoner records. In his commitment to reverently upholding the Way of Heaven, there is nothing left undone. Yet although auspicious signs repeatedly respond, disasters and baneful influences also occur from time to time. I know that the benevolent love of the mind of Heaven perhaps desires that his mind remain the same from beginning to end, in unceasing purity. Then the Four Numina will all arrive, distant peoples communicating through multiple translations will come to pay allegiance to the king, and the seas will be calm and the waves clear—what disasters…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
沴之有哉噫雲漢為虐不害中興天作淫雨
宋其興焉其斯之謂歟愚也迂疎淺陋言無
可采惟執事其進教之
第四問
王岐
同考試官學正盧批五策鑿鑿皆實而人物尤有折衷
遠大之志於此可見矣他日所就豈可量乎
考試官教諭趙批歷數浙之先正無遺其後進之
素知景仰者乎
===
考試官教授戴批先正德業發揚太盡他日所立可知矣
對甚矣人物之鳴世不偶然也關氣運之盛
衰繫吾道之升降其生也有所自其出也有
所為顯道德於當時垂功名於宇宙所以扶
持綱常師表後進於無窮也夫豈偶然哉恭
承執事發策以鄉邦人物下詢承學敢不悉
對且地靈則人傑信如古人之所言也江浙
多人物信如執事之所稱也彼其文武忠孝
人所難全也惟志於道德者有以全之焉觀
punctuated:
沴之有哉！噫！雲漢為虐，不害中興；天作淫雨，宋其興焉，其斯之謂歟！愚也迂疎淺陋，言無可采，惟執事其進教之。
第四問
王岐
〔同考試官學正盧批：五策鑿鑿皆實，而人物尤有折衷，遠大之志於此可見矣，他日所就豈可量乎！〕
〔考試官教諭趙批：歷數浙之先正無遺，其後進之素知景仰者乎！〕
〔考試官教授戴批：先正德業，發揚太盡，他日所立可知矣。〕
對：甚矣，人物之鳴世不偶然也！關氣運之盛衰，繫吾道之升降。其生也有所自，其出也有所為。顯道德於當時，垂功名於宇宙，所以扶持綱常、師表後進於無窮也，夫豈偶然哉！恭承執事發策，以鄉邦人物下詢承學，敢不悉對？且「地靈則人傑」，信如古人之所言也；「江浙多人物」，信如執事之所稱也。彼其文武忠孝，人所難全也，惟志於道德者有以全之焉。觀
translation_en:
…disasters and anomalies could there still be? Alas! Though the Milky Way shone down in a cruel drought, it did not hinder the Zhou restoration; though Heaven sent down excessive rains, the state of Song flourished thereby—is this not what is meant here? Ignorant as I am, pedantic, superficial, and shallow, my words have nothing worthy of adoption; I pray only that Your Excellency will advance and instruct me.

Fourth Question
Wang Qi 王岐
[Comment by Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Comparative Literature Instructor (xuezheng) Lu: All five policy essays are well-grounded and substantial, and the one on eminent figures is especially well-balanced in its judgments. His far-reaching ambitions can be seen right here; how could his future achievements be measured?]
[Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies (jiaoyu) Zhao: He enumerates the former worthies of Zhejiang without omission. Truly a junior scholar who has long known how to look up to and revere them!]
[Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies (jiaoshou) Dai: The moral virtue and achievements of the former worthies are expounded in the fullest detail; what he himself will establish in the future can be known from this.]

I reply: Profound indeed is the fact that eminent figures make their mark in the world not by mere chance! They are bound up with the flourishing and decline of the cosmic cycle, and tied to the rise and fall of our Way. Their birth has its origin, and their coming forth into public life has its purpose. Making moral virtue manifest in their own time and handing down meritorious renown throughout the universe, they thereby uphold the Three Bonds and Five Constant Virtues and serve as models for later generations without end—how could this be by mere chance? Having respectfully received the policy question posed by Your Excellency, which condescends to inquire of a junior student regarding the eminent figures of our native region, how dare I not reply in full? Moreover, that "where the land is numinous, the people are outstanding" is truly as the ancients said; and that "the Jiangzhe region abounds in eminent figures" is truly as Your Excellency has stated. Now, civil and martial achievements, loyalty and filial piety—these are things difficult for a person to bring to perfection all together; only those who set their minds on the Way and its virtue have the means to bring them to perfection. When we observe…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
其倡道於婺而為一代之宗師則東萊吕氏
祖謙也隱居著書以淑斯文之後進則仁山
金氏履祥也少有竒氣而中武舉異等者非
東陽王霆而何生有竒志而第武舉絶倫者
非西安徐徽言而何以至沈與求為御史中
丞而知無不言宜乎謚忠敏焉王萬為監察
御史而彈劾不避宜乎謚忠惠焉陳天隱至
孝聞世而門有八字之旌非所以激勵風俗
乎仰忻孝廉表坊而身應八行之舉非所以
===
拔用真才乎若夫將相公侯人所難致也惟
志於功名者有以致之焉觀夫為將在軍旅
而親賢接士凌統之重義可嘉也為將三十
年而家無長物吕公約之薄取可尚也論諫
甚切一本於仁義者唐陸贄之相業可稱薦
用人材不以私害公者宋史浩之相業無忝
封郇國公而陪葬獻陵錢九隴之生死何榮
幸耶封鄖國公而卒謚威烈杜建徽之始終
何全美耶陳之杜稜封永成侯而配饗武帝
punctuated:
其倡道於婺而為一代之宗師，則東萊吕氏祖謙也；隱居著書以淑斯文之後進，則仁山金氏履祥也。少有竒氣而中武舉異等者，非東陽王霆而何？生有竒志而第武舉絶倫者，非西安徐徽言而何？以至沈與求為御史中丞而知無不言，宜乎謚忠敏焉；王萬為監察御史而彈劾不避，宜乎謚忠惠焉。陳天隱至孝聞世而門有八字之旌，非所以激勵風俗乎？仰忻孝廉表坊而身應八行之舉，非所以拔用真才乎？
若夫將相公侯，人所難致也，惟志於功名者有以致之焉。觀夫為將在軍旅而親賢接士，凌統之重義可嘉也；為將三十年而家無長物，吕公約之薄取可尚也。論諫甚切、一本於仁義者，唐陸贄之相業可稱；薦用人材、不以私害公者，宋史浩之相業無忝。封郇國公而陪葬獻陵，錢九隴之生死何榮幸耶！封鄖國公而卒謚威烈，杜建徽之始終何全美耶！陳之杜稜封永成侯而配饗武帝，
translation_en:
…he who championed the Way in Wu 婺 [Jinhua] and became the grand master of an era was Lü Zuqian 呂祖謙 [Donglai 東萊]; he who lived in seclusion writing books to cultivate later generations in This Culture was Jin Lüxiang 金履祥 [Renshan 仁山]. Who else but Wang Ting 王霆 of Dongyang 東陽 possessed extraordinary spirit in his youth and passed the Military Examination in an exceptional grade? Who else but Xu Huiyan 徐徽言 of Xi'an 西安 [Quzhou] was born with extraordinary ambition and passed the Military Examination in the peerless class? And then there was Shen Yuqiu 沈與求, who as Vice Censor-in-Chief spoke out on everything he knew—how fitting that he received the posthumous title Zhongmin 忠敏 ("Loyal andKeen")! And Wang Wan 王萬, who as Investigating Censor shrank from nothing in his impeachments—how fitting that he received the posthumous title Zhonghui 忠惠 ("Loyal and Benevolent")! Chen Tianyin 陳天隱 was renowned in the world for his utmost filiality and had his gate honored with an eight-character inscription—was this not a means to inspire and encourage public customs? Yang Xin 仰忻 had an archway erected in his honor for being Filial and Incorrupt and personally answered the recommendation for the Eight Conducts—was this not a means to select and employ genuine talent?

As for becoming a general, Chief Councilor, duke, or marquis, these are ranks difficult for men to attain; only those who set their minds on merit and fame have the means to attain them. Observe how, as a general on campaign, Ling Tong 凌統 drew close to the worthy and welcomed scholars—his emphasis on righteousness is praiseworthy; and how, after serving as a general for thirty years, Lü Gongyue 呂公約 had no surplus possessions at home—his modesty in taking is admirable. In offering remonstrances that were deeply incisive and rooted entirely in humanity and righteousness, the ministerial achievements of Lu Zhi 陸贄 of the Tang are worthy of praise; in recommending and employing men of talent without letting private interests harm the public good, the ministerial achievements of Shi Hao 史浩 of the Song are without blemish. Enfeoffed as Duke of Xun 郇國公 and accorded an attendant burial at the Xian Mausoleum 獻陵, how glorious and fortunate was Qian Jiulong 錢九隴 in both life and death! Enfeoffed as Duke of Yun 鄖國公 and given the posthumous title Weilie 威烈 ("Majestic and Martial") upon his death, how complete and admirable was Du Jianhui 杜建徽 from beginning to end! As for Du Leng 杜稜 of the Chen dynasty, who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yongcheng 永成侯 and enshrined as an associate recipient of sacrifices in the temple of Emperor Wu 武帝…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
死而得寵也為何如吳之朱治封毗陵侯而
恩敬極隆生而得君也為何如夫語數君子
之道德則道濟天下德被生民固後學所當
勉也等而上之孔孟顏曾之道德皆吾性中
物耳敢不于是而取法乎語數君子之功名
則功銘鼎彝名垂竹帛固後學所當仰也推
而極之伊傅周召之功名皆吾分內事耳敢
不于是而期望乎愚也後生小子於鄉邦之
人物未能徧觀而盡識於聖賢之事業未能
身體而力行姑因明問所及而槩陳之惟恕
其狂斐而進教焉
第五問
謝遷
同考試官教諭朱批處置得宜足見學識
考試官教諭趙批因時制宜各當其可使見
之行事必有可觀者焉
考試官教授戴批有用之才觀此策可見矣是宜錄出
嘗聞善為政者莫先於立法善立法者莫要
punctuated:
死而得寵也為何如！吳之朱治封毗陵侯而恩敬極隆，生而得君也為何如！夫語數君子之道德，則道濟天下、德被生民，固後學所當勉也；等而上之，孔、孟、顏、曾之道德，皆吾性中物耳，敢不于是而取法乎？語數君子之功名，則功銘鼎彝、名垂竹帛，固後學所當仰也；推而極之，伊、傅、周、召之功名，皆吾分內事耳，敢不于是而期望乎？愚也後生小子，於鄉邦之人物未能徧觀而盡識，於聖賢之事業未能身體而力行，姑因明問所及而槩陳之，惟恕其狂斐而進教焉。

第五問
謝遷
同考試官教諭朱批：處置得宜，足見學識。
考試官教諭趙批：因時制宜，各當其可，使見之行事，必有可觀者焉。
考試官教授戴批：有用之才，觀此策可見矣，是宜錄出。

嘗聞善為政者莫先於立法，善立法者莫要
translation_en:
… how great was the favor he enjoyed after death! And as for Zhu Zhi 朱治 of Wu, who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Piling 毗陵 and treated with the utmost grace and respect, how great was the sovereign's confidence he enjoyed in life! Now, if we speak of the Way and virtue of these several gentlemen—their Way benefiting all under Heaven and their virtue extending to the common people—they are indeed what later scholars ought to strive to emulate. Yet ascending a step higher, the Way and virtue of Confucius 孔子, Mencius 孟子, Yan Hui 顏回, and Zengzi 曾子 are all things inherent in our own nature; how could we dare not take them as our model? And if we speak of the achievements and fame of these several gentlemen—their achievements inscribed on tripods and sacrificial vessels and their names handed down on bamboo and silk—they are indeed what later scholars ought to look up to. Yet pushing this to the ultimate, the achievements and fame of Yi Yin 伊尹, Fu Yue 傅說, the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Duke of Shao 召公 are all matters within our own proper duty; how could we dare not set our hopes upon them? Stupid and a mere youth of the younger generation as I am, I have not yet been able to survey broadly and know thoroughly the notable figures of our home region, nor have I been able to personally embody and earnestly practice the enterprises of the sages and worthies. For the moment, following what Your enlightened question has touched upon, I set forth this general account, praying only that You will pardon my rashness and crudity and grant me further instruction.

Fifth Question
Xie Qian 謝遷
Associate Examiner Instructor Zhu 朱 comments: His handling of matters is appropriate, sufficing to show his learning and insight.
Examiner Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: Adapting measures to the times, each is suited to what is proper; if put into actual practice, there would surely be much worth seeing in it.
Examiner Professor Dai 戴 comments: A man of useful talent, as can be seen from examining this policy essay; it ought to be selected for publication.

I have heard that for those skilled in governing, nothing comes before establishing laws, and for those skilled in establishing laws, nothing is more essential…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
於得人盖法因人而後行也有其法而又有
其人則令行政舉而民受其福矣孔子曰為
政在人良有以夫請因明問而條陳之為政
之法固非一端而其要則有五焉五者何曰
訓農桑曰省賦役曰簡詞訟曰厚風俗曰弭
盜賊是已是故百畝之田勿奪其時五畝之
宅樹之以桑三代之時農有餘粟而女有餘
布矣今之田畝不減於古而民之衣食反不
足者無他盖由訓農桑者之不得其人耳苟
===
得其人以任其責則必巡行阡陌而盡勞来
之方命具籧筐而戒游惰之弊將見男樂於
耕女勤於織而衣食何患乎不足歌大田之
詩徂東山之役三代之民薄已奉上趨事赴
工矣今之賦役不繁於古而民之生理反不
遂者無他盖由省賦役者之不得其人耳苟
得其人以司其事則必薄其稅斂使無橫征
之政平其傜役俾無愁嘆之苦將見出納有
經勞逸適均而生理何患乎不遂詞訟非不
punctuated:
於得人，盖法因人而後行也。有其法而又有其人，則令行政舉而民受其福矣。孔子曰：「為政在人。」良有以夫！請因明問而條陳之。

為政之法固非一端，而其要則有五焉。五者何？曰訓農桑，曰省賦役，曰簡詞訟，曰厚風俗，曰弭盜賊是已。是故百畝之田，勿奪其時；五畝之宅，樹之以桑。三代之時，農有餘粟而女有餘布矣。今之田畝不減於古，而民之衣食反不足者，無他，盖由訓農桑者之不得其人耳。苟得其人以任其責，則必巡行阡陌而盡勞来之方，命具籧筐而戒游惰之弊，將見男樂於耕、女勤於織，而衣食何患乎不足？歌《大田》之詩，徂東山之役，三代之民，薄已奉上，趨事赴工矣。今之賦役不繁於古，而民之生理反不遂者，無他，盖由省賦役者之不得其人耳。苟得其人以司其事，則必薄其稅斂，使無橫征之政；平其傜役，俾無愁嘆之苦。將見出納有經、勞逸適均，而生理何患乎不遂？詞訟非不
translation_en:
… than obtaining the right men, for laws take effect only through men. When one has the right laws and also has the right men, orders are carried out, administration flourishes, and the people enjoy the blessings thereof. Confucius said, "Governance lies in men." Truly there is good reason for this! Allow me to set forth my views item by item in response to your enlightened question.

The methods of governance are certainly not limited to a single aspect, yet their essentials come down to five. What are the five? They are: instructing in agriculture and sericulture, lightening taxes and labor services, simplifying litigation, enriching customs, and suppressing banditry. Thus, when the seasons of the hundred-mu fields were not encroached upon and the five-mu homesteads were planted with mulberry trees, in the time of the Three Dynasties farmers had surplus grain and women had surplus cloth. That the acreage of fields today is no less than in antiquity, and yet the people's clothing and food are on the contrary insufficient, is for no other reason than that those who instruct in agriculture and sericulture have not been the right men. If we obtain the right men to shoulder this responsibility, they will surely tour the field paths and exhaust every means of encouragement and comfort, and order the preparation of silkworm trays and baskets while warning against the abuses of idleness and sloth. Then we shall see men rejoicing in plowing and women diligent in weaving—what worry would there be of clothing and food being insufficient? Singing the ode "Great Fields" (Datian) and marching on the campaigns to the Eastern Hills (Dongshan), the people of the Three Dynasties stinted themselves to serve their superiors and hastened to their duties and works. That taxes and labor services today are no heavier than in antiquity, and yet the people's livelihood is on the contrary unfulfilled, is for no other reason than that those who lighten taxes and labor services have not been the right men. If we obtain the right men to take charge of these matters, they will surely reduce taxes and levies so that there is no tyrannical extraction in governance, and equalize corvée labor so that there is no bitter sighing in distress. Then we shall see revenue and expenditure regulated by constant norms, labor and rest properly balanced—what worry would there be of livelihoods going unfulfilled? As for litigation, it is not that we do not…

title: 成化十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
欲簡也然而一邑之小日至數百何多耶必
欲如古之虞芮質成於文王之化兄弟感義
於蘇瓊之政者非得其人奚可哉得其人而
任之則有德化以為息訟之本明決以為聽
訟之具由是惡者善而枉者伸詞訟其有不
簡者乎風俗非不欲厚也然而十室之邑鮮
聞忠信何薄耶必欲如古之仁義薰蒸而比
屋有可封之俗禮樂甄陶而人人有君子之
風者非得其人又奚可哉得其人而用之則
===
興學校納斯民於衣冠之鄉明禮義置斯民
於弦歌之地由是鄙夫敦而薄夫寬風俗其
有不厚者乎若乃盜賊者飢寒之所迫非不
欲息也然而小則穿窬攘奪大則蜂屯蟻聚
又安得如唐貞觀之時山行水宿而外戶不
閉歟亦惟在於得人而已得其人焉吾見道
之以德齊之以禮使之有以勸於善道之以
政齊之以刑使之有以懲其惡如是則向之
穿窬攘奪者今則化而為良善之歸昔之蜂
punctuated: 欲簡也，然而一邑之小，日至數百，何多耶？必欲如古之虞、芮質成於文王之化，兄弟感義於蘇瓊之政者，非得其人奚可哉？得其人而任之，則有德化以為息訟之本，明決以為聽訟之具，由是惡者善而枉者伸，詞訟其有不簡者乎？風俗非不欲厚也，然而十室之邑，鮮聞忠信，何薄耶？必欲如古之仁義薰蒸，而比屋有可封之俗；禮樂甄陶，而人人有君子之風者，非得其人又奚可哉？得其人而用之，則興學校，納斯民於衣冠之鄉；明禮義，置斯民於弦歌之地。由是鄙夫敦而薄夫寬，風俗其有不厚者乎？若乃盜賊者，飢寒之所迫，非不欲息也，然而小則穿窬攘奪，大則蜂屯蟻聚，又安得如唐貞觀之時，山行水宿而外戶不閉歟？亦惟在於得人而已。得其人焉，吾見道之以德，齊之以禮，使之有以勸於善；道之以政，齊之以刑，使之有以懲其惡。如是，則向之穿窬攘奪者，今則化而為良善之歸；昔之蜂
translation_en:
…desired to be kept simple; yet in a single small district they reach several hundred a day—why are there so many? If one wishes it to be as in antiquity, when the states of Yu 虞 and Rui 芮 settled their dispute through the transforming influence of King Wen 文王, or when brothers were moved to righteousness by the governance of Su Qiong 蘇瓊, how could this be possible without obtaining the right men? Once one obtains the right men and entrusts them with office, there will be moral transformation as the root of ending litigation, and clear decisiveness as the instrument for hearing lawsuits. Thereby the wicked will become good and the wronged will be redressed—how then could lawsuits fail to become simple?

As for customs, it is not that they are not desired to be generous; yet in a hamlet of ten households one rarely hears of loyalty and trustworthiness—why are they so shallow? If one wishes it to be as in antiquity, when benevolence and righteousness permeated everywhere so that every household side by side had customs worthy of enfeoffment, and when rites and music molded the people so that everyone had the demeanor of a gentleman, how again could this be possible without obtaining the right men? Once one obtains the right men and employs them, they will promote schools and bring the people into a community of caps and robes, and they will clarify rites and righteousness and place the people in a land of stringed instruments and singing. Thereby the mean man will become sincere and the shallow man magnanimous—how then could customs fail to become generous?

As for bandits and thieves, driven as they are by hunger and cold, it is not that one does not desire to put an end to them; yet on a small scale they bore through walls and seize goods, and on a large scale they swarm like bees and gather like ants. How can we attain a state like that of the Zhenguan 貞觀 era (627–649) of the Tang 唐, when travelers journeyed through mountains and lodged by waters and outer doors were left unbolted? This too lies solely in obtaining the right men. Once the right men are obtained, I see that they will lead the people with virtue and regulate them with rites, giving them the means to be encouraged toward goodness; and they will lead them with administrative injunctions and regulate them with punishments, giving them the means to be deterred from evil. Thus, those who formerly bored through walls and seized goods will now be transformed and return to being good citizens, while those who in the past swarmed like bees…
